documents.abstract: Abstract—The exponential scaling of frontier Artificial Intelligence (AI) foundation models and global real-time inference workloads has precipitated an alarming surge in electrical energy consumption, water cooling demands, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Training a single 70B+ parameter transformer model consumes hundreds of megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity, while high-throughput inference serving clusters run continuous multi-kilowatt server racks across worldwide datacenters. In response, 'Green AI' has emerged as an essential computational discipline prioritizing energy efficiency, operational and embodied carbon footprint minimization, and computational sustainability alongside raw accuracy metrics ('Red AI'). However, transitioning enterprise computing systems toward sustainable AI introduces multifaceted engineering trade-offs: algorithmic compression vs. downstream reasoning degradation, non-uniform spatial-temporal grid carbon intensity, and memory bandwidth bottlenecks under low-precision quantization. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical survey and empirical architectural evaluation of Green AI spanning the entire lifecycle of foundation models. We formalize the holistic carbon accounting framework incorporating embodied silicon manufacturing emissions, model the mathematical dynamics of dynamic Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) token routing, analyze FlashAttention memory-IO energy bounds, and formulate carbon-aware spatiotemporal workload scheduling across geographically distributed datacenters. Furthermore, we construct an empirical enterprise benchmarking testbed across an 8-node NVIDIA H100/A100 cluster executing pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference on open foundation models (Llama-3-70B, Mixtral-8x7B). Our empirical findings demonstrate that sparse MoE routing paired with FP8 FlashAttention-3 slashes pre-training energy consumption by 48.2% while matching dense model perplexity. Concurrently, carbon-aware temporal job shifting achieves a 38.6% reduction in operational carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions by aligning elastic training runs with regional renewable grid surpluses. Finally, we formulate open challenges in zero-water datacenter cooling, unified embodied carbon lifecycle tracking, and sustainable microarchitectural hardware co-design. Index Terms—Green AI, Sustainable Computing, Carbon Accounting, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), FlashAttention, Speculative Decoding, Spatiotemporal Workload Scheduling, Energy-Efficient Deep Learning.

The explosive growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has allowed connecting everywhere in the healthcare, smart city, agriculture, and industry areas. Nevertheless, the rapid increase in the launch of IoT ecosystem presents essential issues of data privacy, security, trust, and interoperability. The potential of blockchain technology to solve the problem has become one of the prospects of this technology, as it is decentralized, immutable, and transparent. However, traditional blockchain systems tend to be energy-intensive and computationally intensive, which makes them inappropriate in resource-limited IoT devices with low processing power, storage, and battery capacity. To address this shortcoming green blockchain models have been put forward, with the aim of ensuring energy efficiency, scalability, and sustainability without compromising on the strong security guarantees. This chapter offers an in-depth discussion on energy-efficient blockchain paradigms optimized to be used in IoT systems. It starts with the description of the inherent limitations of IoT devices and the inefficiency of classical consensus mechanisms of blockchains, including Proof-of-Work. The topic then focuses on the lightweight alternatives, such as hybrid consensus protocols, Proof-of-Stake, Delegated Proof-of-Stake, Proof-of-Authority, and ledgers based on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). The importance of edge and fog computing in minimizing the amount of energy spent on the execution of intensive blockchain tasks is also highlighted. Moreover, the chapter reviews real-life examples of green blockchain systems in the medical care monitoring, supply chain management, and smart city systems, in which sustainable and secure data management is essential. The main issues like interoperability within heterogeneous IoT platforms, decentralization versus energy saving trade-offs, and adherence to international sustainability objectives are reviewed critically. Lastly, the chapter also highlights potential research prospects in the future that involve artificial intelligence (AI)-based energy optimization capabilities, cross-chain interoperability systems, and how renewable energy sources can be incorporated into IoT deployments. This research integrates theoretical materials with real-life examples to support the idea of the transformative capability of green blockchain models in the development of IoT ecosystems to a new level of security, sustainability, and energy efficiency.

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into environmental sustainability strategies presents a critical dilemma known as the "Green Tech Paradox." While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to optimize resource allocation, predict climate patterns, and enhance energy efficiency across industrial sectors, its deployment carries substantial, often overlooked, ecological costs. This research provides a critical analysis of the dual role AI plays as both a catalyst for eco-innovations and a significant contributor to environmental degradation. On the positive frontier, AI-driven applications accelerate sustainability by enabling smart power grids, improving carbon capture systems, facilitating precision agriculture, and modeling complex environmental crises. Machine learning algorithms enhance operational efficiency, reducing waste and carbon footprints in manufacturing and logistics. However, these beneficial outcomes are counterbalanced by the escalating physical footprint of AI infrastructure. The training and continuous execution of complex neural networks demand massive amounts of electricity, heavily relying on fossil-fuel-dominant energy grids. Furthermore, data centers consume millions of liters of freshwater daily for cooling mechanisms, accelerating localized water scarcity, while the rapid obsolescence of specialized hardware generates growing volumes of hazardous electronic waste. This paper evaluates this structural tension through a multidimensional synthesis of secondary data, life-cycle assessments, and resource consumption metrics across global data centers. The analysis reveals that without stringent regulatory frameworks and sustainable design interventions, the environmental degradation caused by AI's hardware lifecycle risks surpassing its ecological benefits. Ultimately, the study advocates for a paradigm shift toward "Green AI"—prioritizing algorithmic efficiency, renewable energy integration for computing infrastructure, sustainable hardware lifecycle management, and policy-driven eco-design standards. By establishing transparent auditing protocols, researchers and industry leaders can mitigate the hidden ecological liabilities of artificial intelligence, ensuring that modern technological advancement aligns genuinely with global net-zero targets and long-term planetary boundaries. Keywords: Green AI, Climate change mitigation, Sustainable development goals (SDGs), Environmental governance, Lifecycle assessment of AI.

Objectives: This study comprehensively investigates the underlying mechanisms through which green transformational leadership and work motivation influence sustainable employee performance. Specifically, the research evaluates the pivotal mediating role of employee engagement within the highly analytical and bureaucratic environment of Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank. Methodology: We employed an explanatory quantitative research design utilizing a cross-sectional survey approach. The empirical data were collected from a carefully determined sample of 158 permanent employees across four strategic departments at Bank Indonesia using a stratified random sampling approach. To test the complex structural relationships and mediation effects, we applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using the SmartPLS 4 software, executing a rigorous bootstrapping procedure with 5,000 subsamples. Finding: The empirical analysis reveals a compelling theoretical anomaly where green transformational leadership does not directly drive sustainable employee performance. Conversely, intrinsic work motivation exerts a strong, positive, and direct impact on the sustainability of employee performance. More importantly, both green leadership and work motivation are highly effective in cultivating deep employee engagement. Consequently, employee engagement emerges as a significant driver of sustainable performance, acting as a full mediator for green transformational leadership and a partial mediator for work motivation. Conclusion: Employee engagement functions as an absolute psychological bridge in a central banking context. Without this deep emotional and cognitive involvement, top-down environmental leadership visions and latent intrinsic motivation cannot effectively materialize into resilient, long-term sustainable performance.

Abstract Hera is an ESA contribution to the international planetary defense effort. It is a deep‐space mission to the binary asteroid system Didymos and Dimorphos, designed to investigate the effects of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), demonstrate autonomous navigation, and support close‐proximity investigation by two CubeSats. Hera includes a Spacecraft Monitoring Camera (SMC) for situational awareness during critical operations such as CubeSat deployments. Although not a science instrument, the SMC may also provide scientifically useful and outreach imagery. Integration was challenging because the SMC uses a private Packet Utilisation Standard (PUS) Type 210 service, was not modeled in the Hera spacecraft simulator, and was initially unsupported by the spacecraft Central Software (CSW). To enable early testing, a ground toolchain was developed for command generation, telemetry extraction, image reassembly, and PNG conversion. Without direct onboard support, commands and telemetry were encapsulated in PUS Service 2 packets, enabling test‐bench integration. Synthetic telemetry was used to validate the processing chain before restricted hardware access. Bench testing revealed a SpaceWire flow‐control anomaly that could stall the affected communication path, so planned SMC imaging during Hera's March 2025 Mars gravity‐assist flyby was canceled. The issue was subsequently addressed in a later flight‐software version, with cruise‐phase validation planned before asteroid proximity operations. This case shows how low‐level ground access, synthetic data, and staged testing can reduce the risk of deferring non‐launch‐critical onboard functionality until after launch.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed the dynamic of energy sustainability across the globe with regard to digital transformation. This chapter discusses AI and renewable energy systems convergence as the basis of smart, low-carbon societies. It discusses the ways in which machine learning, predictive analytics, and digital twins can be used to increase solar, wind, hydropower, bioenergy and geothermal resource forecasting, operational efficiency, fault detection and grid integration. The specific emphasis is put upon AI-driven solutions to intermittency, stabilizing smart grids, and optimizing energy distribution and demand management. The chapter, as well, assesses the increasing energy requirements of AI infrastructures and suggests ways of creating energy-efficient, low-carbon AI architectures. It combines the technical, environmental, and policy views to put the practical uses providing resilience and net-zero transitions and focus on governance, ethics, and responsible innovation to promote sustainable and inclusive development.

We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

Hemolytic illness, an immune-mediated disease that can be fatal, is brought on by maternal alloantibodies against fetal red blood cell antigens inherited from the father. Fetal anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, hydrops fetalis, and, in extreme circumstances, perinatal mortality these placental-crossing maternal immunoglobulin G antibodies. The incidence of RhD linked HDFN has decreased significantly, however alloimmunization against other blood group antigens such Kell, Rh c, Rh E, Duffy, Kidd, and ABO antigens still causes clinically significant disease. Thus, HDFN remains a significant concern in the fields of immunohematology, transfusion medicine, obstetrics, and neonatology. This review aims to present the current knowledge of the immunohematological mechanism of maternal alloimmunization and fetal hemolysis, especially focusing on clinically important blood group systems and antibody characteristics. Recent prenatal diagnostic developments, There have been notable advancements in early diagnosis and risk stratification of affected pregnancies because of advancements in technology like MCA-PSV Doppler ultrasound, molecular immunohematology, high throughput genotyping, and cell-free fetal DNA for non-invasive fetal blood type genotyping. Newer management techniques, including serial maternal antibody monitoring, intrauterine transfusion, optimized timing of delivery, neonatal phototherapy, exchange transfusion and evidence-based transfusion support, have dramatically improved the survival of fetuses and minimized disease-related complications. In addition, new technologies and innovations such as those based on artificial intelligence that can predict risk, digital immunohematology, automated compatibility testing, FcRn inhibitors, complement targeted therapies, and personalized immunotherapeutic strategies will help further define the diagnosis and management of HDFN. Nevertheless, the world faces many obstacles to achieving these advances, including the lack of access to molecular diagnostics, availability of appropriate blood products, and unequal distribution of health care services. Further multidisciplinary teamwork, technological innovations, and standardized clinical approaches will play a key role in furthering the goals of precision medicine and improving maternal and neonatal outcomes in the management of HDFN.

With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for UI/UX evaluation and design decision support; however, their responses are often generated as implicit and unstructured outputs, making cognitive processes and judgment rationale difficult to trace. Moreover, the quality of LLM-based judgments may vary depending on users’ prompting proficiency, limiting the consistency of AI-assisted evaluation. This study proposes HIPA (Human Information Processing Architecture), a cognitive response architecture that structures LLM outputs based on the human information processing (HIP) model and investigates the manifestation of human cognitive stages in conventional LLM responses. HIPA maps four HIP stages—perception, working memory, decision making, and response execution—into a two-stage response structure consisting of information provision and judgment support through knowledge-grounded prompting with GPT-4o. An exploratory evaluation was conducted with seven participants with different prompting proficiency levels who assessed the same mobile login interface using a general LLM. Responses were coded according to HIP-stage manifestation using a three-point scale. The results showed that perception and response execution were consistently observed, whereas working memory and decision-making stages varied depending on prompt systematicity. These findings indicate that general LLM responses do not inherently provide cognitively structured judgment support. HIPA provides a human-centered framework for developing AI-assisted UI/UX evaluation systems based on human cognitive principles.

Human factors and ergonomics (HFE) is vital for optimising human-centred system design. This study aimed to synthesise research on HFE and examine its historical evolution, current landscape and emerging trends. A bibliometric analysis and a knowledge-domain mapping analysis were conducted to combine perspectives on journal development and article output. This study focused on 24 journals classified in the ergonomics category in the Journal Citation Reports of 2024. Critical information for the 24 HFE journals was investigated, including commencement year of publication, composition of editorial boards, number of published papers, publishing models, 2024 quartile rankings and impact factors and 5-year impact factors. Two visualisation tools, VOSviewer and CiteSpace, were used to perform the bibliometric analysis of the 26,026 HFE documents in the Web of Science Core Collection, spanning 2010 to 2024. Results showed that HFE literature has evolved from classical industrial origins to modern technological paradigms. Increased collaborations across different research areas to address HFE problems were observed. The review also identified key domain expansions across high-impact emerging HFE frontiers, including artificial intelligence, extended reality, autonomous vehicles and wearable technologies. Building upon these findings, the study may provide in-depth insights into the critical future HFE research directions.

While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 42.2% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 83.0% of traces. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.

Purpose Based on the self-determination theory, this study aims to examine the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which the use of artificial intelligence sales technology (AIST) shapes sales performance. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 conducted a questionnaire survey of 396 sales employees and their supervisors in China’s real estate industry. Study 2 adopted a time-lagged research design involving 324 sales employees in various industries and their immediate supervisors. Regression analyses with Mplus 8.3 were performed to test the hypotheses. Findings The empirical results indicate that the use of AIST indirectly influences sales performance through the mediating roles of the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence and relatedness. Furthermore, salespeople’s performance goal orientation attenuates the positive relationship between AIST usage and the satisfaction of salespeople’s needs for competence and relatedness. Originality/value This study advances the emerging literature on the effectiveness of AIST usage by revealing the psychological pathways through which AIST influences sales performance and offers practical insights for strengthening AI–human collaboration in the workplace.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in socially interactive roles, with virtual influencers emerging as a prominent form of AI‐mediated communication. This study examines how consumers engage with agents that simulate social presence yet lack independent agency. Using a mixed‐methods design, we investigate how authenticity, transparency, and privacy concerns relate to trust, acceptance, and responsibility attribution. The findings show that consumer responses cannot be reduced to trust formation alone. Instead, individuals evaluate whether engagement remains acceptable under conditions of artificial agency. Authenticity supports trust by providing coherence, while transparency and privacy concerns introduce competing interpretations related to control and risk. Privacy concerns are also associated with greater responsibility attribution to brands and developers. These results suggest that engagement with virtual influencers can be interpreted as a process in which consumers negotiate trust and accountability. The study offers an integrated perspective on AI‐mediated influence and highlights the role of distributed responsibility in shaping consumer responses.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) presents an opportunity to transform neonatal care. By rapidly assimilating large volumes of complex, multi-dimensional data to produce real-time predictions, machine learning (ML) models have the potential to enable personalised monitoring and treatment and earlier intervention. This narrative review aims to provide clinicians with a foundational overview of AI and its potential role in the care of preterm infants, with a particular focus on respiratory pathologies. We introduce different types of AI tools and ways to assess predictive model performance. We summarise existing literature using AI and conventional predictive models to predict respiratory conditions, including extubation readiness, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and apnoea occurrence and risk. Finally, we discuss current limitations of AI in neonatology, barriers to clinical translation and the next steps needed to overcome them. These may include multicentre collaboration and data sharing, using dynamic inputs such as vital signs to reflect evolving physiology, and improved transparency, accessibility and training for clinicians, as well as clear guidelines for clinical application, accountability and ongoing monitoring.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BackgroundAutomation, including both robots and AI, are increasingly implemented in the public sector to handle an increased demand for services while facing a shortage of staff. However, little is known of how automation is related to employees' work characteristics and well-being.ObjectiveThe purpose of the present study was to examine how automation is related to work characteristics and well-being in a national sample of social workers.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted with a sample of 1428 social workers in Sweden, comparing those working with automation technologies (e.g., robotization in terms of automated decision-making support in financial aid) to those without.ResultsThe findings indicate that automation is negatively related to relational aspects of work, such as beneficiary contact and social support, and increases perceived workload and role conflict. However, no significant differences were found on decision-making autonomy, role clarity, or skill variety. Despite these work design changes, no significant differences in well-being outcomes, such as burnout and vigor, were observed between the two groups.ConclusionThe findings suggest that automation may alter the nature of social work without necessarily changing employee well-being. These insights have implications for organizations seeking to implement automation in a way that supports employees' work experience and well-being.

People increasingly bring their health questions to ChatGPT, yet safety evaluations of LLM health advice rest almost entirely on clinician-authored vignettes, synthetic prompts, or simulated user profiles. The gap is widest for the Global South, where concerns about demographic bias and unsafe recommendations are well documented but have never been tested on real usage. We present, to our knowledge, the first demographically grounded safety evaluation of real-world health conversations with ChatGPT. From a consent-based data-donation corpus of 202,590 conversations from 1,252 users in India, Nigeria, Brazil, and Pakistan (December 2022 to February 2026), each linked to self-reported age and gender, we identify 15,555 health conversations, classify their health intent using an LLM classifier adapted from an established taxonomy, and score response safety under both a context-blind and a user-context-aware rubric. Roughly one in five health conversations receives a high-risk rating. Risk concentrates in symptom and condition queries and recurs through identifiable failure modes: unsafe medication or dosage guidance, harmful self-diagnosis, missing safety warnings, encouraging over-reliance on the model, and failure to refer users to professionals. Supplying the user's own accumulated context raises the high-risk share by 13-17 percentage points, and about one in four conversations rated safe in isolation turns out to be unsafe for the specific person asking. Safety evaluations built on synthetic cases are likely to miss these harms.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Pfeffer, Krügel, and Uhl (2025) report that OpenAI’s reasoning model o1-mini produces more utilitarian responses to the trolley problem and footbridge dilemma than the non-reasoning model GPT-4o, and they raise the question whether growing reasoning capabilities bring about a “utilitarian turn” in LLMs. I extend their exploratory study in a direction they call for: with four current OpenAI models and systematic prompt variation. On the trolley dilemma, the hypothesized utilitarian turn is not confirmed. GPT-4o’s low utilitarian rate reflects safety refusals triggered by the prompt’s advisory framing rather than a deontological commitment; on reformulated prompt variants—for instance, agent-neutral “Is it morally permissible…?” instead of advisory “Should I…?”—all four models, reasoning or not, converge on utilitarian answers. The footbridge finding is partially confirmed: reasoning models tend to give more utilitarian responses than non-reasoning models across prompt variations, but they often refuse to answer or answer non-utilitarian. These results demonstrate that single-prompt evaluations of LLM moral responses are unreliable: multi-prompt robustness testing should be standard practice for any empirical claims about LLM behavior.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: The innovation ecosystem is expressed in the form of a network system that plays an important role in the economic development of countries in the 21st century.It is necessary to consider the innovation ecosystem in a way as an innovative environment in creation of which all sides implementing innovative work and service processes-governmental and non-governmental organizations, commercial associations and, most importantly, human capital are involved.Human capital, which refers to the skills, knowledge, experience and creativity of individuals within society, is a key driver of innovation and a fundamental element in fostering a dinamic and sustainable innovation ecosystem.The human factor encourages the generation of ideas, entrepreneurship, collaboration and knowledge creation, contributing to the development of innovative solutions and the economic and social progress of a region or country.The research study investigated the role and importance of human capital in the innovation ecosystem, which is a particularly important factor in the modern world of information and digitization, where the main focus is on the "brain product".The result of researchers who have studied the mentioned topic before, are analyzed during the research, and the statistical data is used as the main data supporting the hypothesis.

The purpose of the research -This article examines human capital assessment through the integration of heterogeneous data and artificial intelligence in the context of the digital economy.The study aims to identify the interrelationships among artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and human capital, and to empirically evaluate how these factors influence productivity. Research methodology -The research applies analysis, comparison, systematization, grouping, and generalization methods.Its empirical part is based on panel data covering the period 2010-2024 and obtained from open international statistical databases.The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, unit root tests, cointegration analysis, multivariate regression modeling, and Granger causality testing.This methodological approach allows a comprehensive assessment of the interaction between artificial intelligence, digital transformation, human capital, and productivity.Results of the research -The findings show that artificial intelligence has a significant positive impact on productivity, while human capital strongly reinforces this effect.Digital transformation also contributes positively through better data processing and resource allocation.The results confirm long-run relationships among the variables and identify artificial intelligence and human capital as major drivers of productivity growth.Originality and scientific novelty of the research -The study offers an integrated and multidimensional framework for evaluating human capital in the digital economy.

This article presents a systematic literature review of the role of human capital in digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on how these developments reshape workforce competencies and human resource management (HRM) during the transition from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0. Following the PRISMA guidelines, the study combines thematic coding with comparative analysis. From an initial pool of 216 publications, 46 studies were selected for in-depth analysis. The review examines how AI and digitalisation change workforce skill requirements and how HRM mechanisms can help organisations develop and sustain the necessary competencies. The findings indicate a shift from routine and manual tasks toward hybrid competency profiles that integrate data analytics skills, AI literacy, human–machine interaction skills, and higher-order socio-cognitive capabilities, including adaptive reasoning, collaboration, and ethical judgement. HRM emerges as a strategic integrator that supports continuous reskilling, predictive skills-gap analysis, and the development of effective human–AI teams. Based on these findings, the study proposes a multilevel framework explaining how institutional mechanisms, organisational strategy, HRM practices, and human–AI complementarity jointly shape workforce competitiveness in AI-enabled digital transformation. The framework contributes to human-centric digitalisation by linking workforce competitiveness to capability velocity and human–AI complementarity. It also provides managerial implications for designing learning, governance, and decision-making structures that enable organisations to respond to evolving competency requirements and translate technological potential into sustainable operational advantages.

Service organizations increasingly employ artificial intelligence and predictive analytics to allocate financial, technological, workforce, and operational resources. Although algorithmic systems can process complex organizational data, purely prediction-driven approaches may generate recommendations that are difficult for managers to interpret, validate, or reconcile with organizational constraints. These limitations become particularly important in healthcare and other information-intensive service environments where resource allocation decisions interact with workforce capacity, digital workflows, privacy requirements, project priorities, and service quality objectives. This study proposes a human centered explainable artificial intelligence framework for adaptive resource allocation and decision governance. The framework integrates predictive modeling, multi objective optimization, and explainability mechanisms within a structured decision support architecture. Rather than optimizing a single performance measure, the proposed approach considers multiple objectives including operational efficiency, resource utilization, service responsiveness, workforce capacity, fairness, and decision transparency. A human-in-the-loop governance mechanism allows decision-makers to review explanations, modify organizational constraints, and evaluate alternative allocation scenarios before recommendations are implemented. Because real organizational data are not used in the present study, the framework is evaluated using synthetically generated operational environments representing variations in demand, workforce availability, resource limitations, project priorities, and unexpected disruptions. Scenario and sensitivity analyses can then examine how resource allocation recommendations change under alternative organizational conditions. The principal contribution is an integrated analytical architecture in which optimization and explainability operate as complementary components of organizational decision making. The proposed framework can provide a foundation for transparent resource allocation systems applicable to healthcare, professional services, digital enterprises, and other service-oriented organizations seeking to improve efficiency and resilience while retaining managerial oversight.

documents.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

Hybrid work has moved from an emergency response to a deliberate work-design option, but its productivity consequences depend on how flexibility and digital coordination are organized. This study examined the relationship between hybrid work model and employee productivity in civil society organizations in Nigeria. Specifically, it assessed the relationship between work-location flexibility and employee productivity and determined the relationship between digital collaboration effectiveness and employee productivity. A survey research design was adopted. The study covered eight selected civil society organizations, with a population of 267 employees whose roles were compatible with hybrid work. A sample of 160 employees was selected, 155 questionnaires were returned and 152 usable responses were analyzed. Work-location flexibility and digital collaboration effectiveness were used as dimensions of the hybrid work model, while employee productivity was measured through task completion, output quality, timeliness, target attainment and work efficiency. The coded questionnaire data were analysed in EViews 10.0, where descriptive statistics were computed and the multiple regression model was estimated at the 5% significance level. The findings showed that work-location flexibility had a significant positive relationship with employee productivity (Coeff. = 0.3881; p-value = 0.0000), while digital collaboration effectiveness also had a significant positive relationship with employee productivity (Coeff. = 0.4552; p value = 0.0000). The model explained approximately 58.5% of the variation in employee productivity. The study concluded that hybrid work improves productivity in civil society organizations when location flexibility is accompanied by reliable digital collaboration, clear work routines and outcome-focused accountability. It recommended that civil society organizations formalize role-based hybrid schedules and strengthen the digital collaboration systems through which distributed employees coordinate tasks, share documents, monitor deadlines and maintain team visibility.

Artificial intelligence (AI) models are capable of generating highly realistic human images with a tendency to stereotypically bias race and gendered features. These models also readily generate emotional faces, but little is known about the perceptual nature of these expressions. To examine if AI-generated facial expressions emulate similar characteristics to human posed stereotypical facial expressions, we compared the perception of emotions from AI generated facial images to classic sets of human actors posing facial emotions in a stereotypical manner. Across two experiments (total N = 648), participants rated AI-generated and human-posed facial expressions on multiple emotion scales. Study 1 focused on expressions generated by Midjourney (N = 498), and Study 2 replicated the experiment using Google’s Nano Banana 2 (N = 150 . Confusion patterns were remarkably similar across Human and AI-generated expressions, and exploratory factor analysis revealed that the underlying dimensional structure of emotion perception was nearly identical for AI-generated and human-posed expressions), demonstrating their generalizability across image-generation models. Interestingly, some AI-generated emotion categories were rated with higher accuracy and reduced confusability than human posed stereotypical expressions, a finding most robust in Nano Banana 2. This suggests that AI-generated expressions are even more stereotypical and intense than stereotypically posed human expressions, a phenomenon we term Hyper-Expressions. Taken together, the findings suggest that generative AI not only captures stereotypical patterns of emotion expression, but also amplifies and biases them. Results are discussed in the context of current debates between basic emotion and constructional theories of emotion perception.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) is characterised by the convergence of new technologies encompassing artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and the Internet of Things (IoT), and these innovations have permeated the everyday lives of young people globally, including in Nigeria. This study explored the level and factors of ICT engagement and knowledge acquisition among undergraduate students in Lagos State University (LASU). A descriptive survey design was adopted. Quantitative data was collected from 1,009 undergraduate students in the Faculties of Science and Social Sciences through an online questionnaire which was distributed through social media platforms, and the data collection spanned three weeks. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies and percentages) with IBM SPSS Statistics version 26. The findings revealed a high level of ICT engagement in academic activities: most respondents actively used digital devices for academic purposes, expressed confidence in using diverse ICT tools, and participated in online discussions and forums. The primary channels of knowledge acquisition combined traditional sources, notably lecture notes and print textbooks, with digital resources such as educational websites, e-books and online databases, while reliance on the university library showed signs of decline. Respondents overwhelmingly perceived that ICT engagement enhances their understanding of course content, broadens their knowledge beyond classroom instruction and contributes to critical thinking skills. The study recommends comprehensive digital literacy programmes, equitable ICT infrastructure and the modernisation of library services to consolidate these gains

Japanese metaverse discourse relies heavily on collective, often prescriptive visions of technoscientific futures. In general, these hyperbolic visions might be similar across the globe, but what about aspects they deliberately gloss over? Driven by this question, I examine Japan’s corporate metaverse discourse, focusing on the rarely thematized aspects of environmental and social sustainability. Based on Jasanoff’s concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, Adloff’s imaginaries of sustainability, and Brause et al.’s SIPC framework, my mixed-method approach identifies metaverse imaginaries through a combination of digital corpora analysis and semi-structured interviews with 14 expert practitioners from Japan. As a result, five sociotechnical imaginaries of sustainability emerge within Japan’s corporate metaverse discourse: anticipation, digital revolution, pragmatism, cultural essentialism, and technosolutionism. My analysis shows that the answers a nascent metaverse is expected to provide with regard to ecological and social crises depend on the type of metaverse we imagine and its relationship with the real world. The findings suggest that Japan’s imaginaries of metaverse sustainability are uniquely situated between an essentialized past, a challenging present, and distant futures, as well as between Japanese particularities and global tech ideologies.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed the capacity of organisations to deliver personalised recommendations, communications, customer service and digital experiences at scale. This study develops and empirically tests a comprehensive model linking AI-based personalisation with customer loyalty through the mechanisms of trust and customer satisfaction, while simultaneously examining AI service quality and privacy concern as contextual factors. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 400 digital-service users through a structured 5-point Likert-scale questionnaire. The analysis encompasses descriptive statistics, reliability testing, KMO and Bartlett's tests, correlation analysis, multiple regression, mediation and moderation analysis, and selected demographic tests. The results demonstrate acceptable internal consistency for all constructs, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from .801 to .865. The KMO value was .916 and Bartlett's test was statistically significant, indicating that the item correlation matrix was suitable for factor-oriented analysis. AI-based personalisation exhibited a positive association with customer loyalty (β = .380, p < .001), explaining 14.4% of its variance in the simple regression. The full regression model explained 42.4% of the variance in loyalty. A bootstrap test of the serial indirect pathway through trust and satisfaction was positive (indirect effect = .060, 95% CI [.040, .085]). Privacy concern significantly moderated the AI personalisation–loyalty relationship (interaction β = .060, p = .040). The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on AI-driven personalisation by demonstrating that trust and satisfaction serve as critical mediating mechanisms, while privacy concerns represent an important boundary condition. Keywords: artificial intelligence; AI personalisation; customer loyalty; trust; customer satisfaction; privacy concern; AI service quality; digital services

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders are highly prevalent among dental practitioners due to sustained static postures and limited visual accessibility. This study examined the effects of three visual aid conditions: naked eye, magnification loupes, and dental operating microscope on operator posture and musculoskeletal risk using a human-factors approach. Ninety practitioners (n = 30 per group) performed standardized clinical tasks, with posture captured using multi-angle high-resolution photography. Ergonomic risk was assessed using the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment, Rapid Entire Body Assessment, and Branson’s Posture Assessment Instrument, and analyzed using one-way analysis of variance with post hoc comparisons. Significant differences were observed across all measures: RULA (F(2,87)=49.14, p<0.001), REBA (F(2,87)=51.97, p<0.001), and PAI (F(2,87)=37.20, p<0.001). The microscope condition showed the lowest ergonomic risk scores (3.10, 2.80, and 3.23, respectively) compared with the naked-eye and loupes conditions. These findings suggest that visual magnification may contribute to improved ergonomic posture, particularly in the neck and trunk regions, and may help reduce musculoskeletal risk during dental procedures.

documents.abstract: Symbolic regression is the problem of finding an expression that fits a dataset. Solving it requires searching a combinatorial space of candidate expressions. Neural symbolic regression can amortize that search by training a model once on synthetic data and then predicting expressions for a new dataset. But existing models still underperform genetic programming on real, noisy data. We argue that the deficit lies in the training rather than in the paradigm, and present RASR (Reinforced Amortized Symbolic Regression), a method with two key changes to the training recipe. First, we design a synthetic prior that narrows the gap with real-world data: inputs come from the prior of a tabular foundation model; constants are sampled bottom-up, conditioned on the data; targets carry heteroscedastic and structured noise; and everything is standardized. Second, we split training into two stages. Supervised pre-training maximizes the token-level likelihood of a reference expression. This is followed by reinforcement-learning post-training that aligns the model with its inference-time use by rewarding held-out fit and penalizing expression size. On the black-box track of SRBench 2.0, RASR achieves the best mean test $R^2$ rank of all evaluated methods. Three RASR variants, trained with different size penalties, make up most of the accuracy-complexity Pareto front. On Strogatz, our method recovers more ground-truth expressions than any baseline, and on Feynman it is competitive with the best-performing methods.

The construction sector is significant due to its numerous stakeholders, high-cost inputs, and its role in meeting the basic needs of communities such as housing and roads. The success of construction projects, their environmental friendliness, and the minimization of workplace accidents are therefore extremely important. The leadership role and attitude of the employer are crucial in this regard. This study examines the associations among inclusive leadership, narcissistic leadership, and green transformational leadership, as well as differences in these leadership scores across groups defined by project success, environmental friendliness, and occupational health and safety (OHS) measures, as perceived by employees. Data obtained through convenience sampling in Turkey were analyzed using the Mann–Whitney U Test and the Spearman Correlation Test. The study revealed that inclusive leadership and green transformational leadership are positively associated with project success, environmental friendliness, and the implementation of OHS measures as perceived by employees, while narcissistic leadership had a negative association.

Purpose This study examines how key Industry 4.0 technologies relate to environmental sustainability performance in supply chains. Specifically, it examines Internet of Things, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, Digital Twin and Cloud Computing, and explores their relative associations with sustainability outcomes using both statistical and machine learning techniques. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected from 268 supply chain and logistics professionals across multiple industries. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software version 31.0.2. Machine learning analysis was carried out using Orange Data Mining to perform feature importance ranking and decision tree modeling, with model performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. Findings Correlation and hierarchical regression analyses reveal no statistically significant association between any individual Industry 4.0 technology and environmental sustainability performance and tested pairwise interaction effects are likewise non-significant. Exploratory machine learning feature rankings order the technologies differently across three methods, and cross-validated models do not outperform a mean-only baseline, indicating no detectable predictive signal in these data. Research limitations/implications The study is based on cross-sectional survey data, which limits causal interpretation and does not capture changes in technology adoption and sustainability performance over time. The sample, although adequate for the applied analyses, is restricted to 268 respondents and may not fully represent all industries and geographical contexts. Future research should use longitudinal designs, larger international samples and additional Industry 4.0 technologies to extend the understanding of digital transformation and sustainability relationships in supply chains. Practical implications The findings caution against expecting sustainability improvements from technology adoption alone. No individual technology, and no tested combination, showed a statistically significant association with environmental sustainability performance, and cross-validated models showed no predictive signal. The results redirect managerial attention from technology acquisition toward the mediating organizational practices through which digital technologies may generate sustainability value. Originality/value This study measures six Industry 4.0 technologies as separate constructs within a single sample, combines conventional statistical testing with exploratory, cross-validated machine learning, and transparently reports a null result for direct technology–performance associations a finding that complements prior mediation-based evidence by suggesting that direct effects of individual technologies may be weak in the absence of mediating capabilities.

documents.abstract: Textiles as clothing predominantly serve as an embodiment of modesty, protection and aesthetics; however, another characteristic being associated with textiles in recent times is the integration of smart features into fabrics to produce the new-age smart textiles. Smart textiles encompass a field of innovation that is deemed to offer versatility and broaden the scope of the traditional textile and apparel products. The state-of-the-art textiles are designed giving precedence to functional attributes in textiles over design and accordingly involve different technologies and innovations to tailor a clothing for specialized applications such as healthcare, protection, safety and leisure activities. Smart textiles exhibit the ability of interacting, responding and adapting in accordance with the changing environment or wearer inputs. The varied domains of smart textiles, namely sportswear, E-textiles or wearable electronics, modular convertible garments, space suits and bio-inspired clothing, are testament to colossal potential and innovation spanning this emerging textile domain. Sportswear is a crucial clothing category popular among sportspersons and fitness freaks that find application in professional sports, athletics and leisure activities. Sports-specific clothing fulfils the wearer’s requirements of comfort, dry feel next to skin, safety and protection from external elements. Sportswear and wearable electronics constitute an indispensable segment of smart textiles. The sportswear is being designed and developed with integration of sensors and electronic components to impart comfort and sport-specific functionality along with smart features like activity tracking and monitoring of wearer’s physiological parameters. Accordingly, several innovative approaches in raw material selection to ergonomics and design features have been experimented and incorporated to develop state-of-the-art smart sportswear. The enhanced and multitude of functionalities are possible with integration of electronics and utilization of computing technologies in sportswear. Nevertheless, the development of smart clothing is a daunting task since designers and manufacturers don’t just have to consider the aesthetic aspects but also the functionality, comfort, durability and easy care associated with smart clothing.

documents.abstract: Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. A user states requirements from their own understanding of the task, and these \textbf{stated requirements} often differ from the \textbf{true requirements} that completing the task imposes. An agent should therefore treat the instruction as evidence rather than as the objective, inferring the true requirements from the instruction and the environment and satisfying them even when the user is not yet aware of all of them. We call this ability \textbf{outcome alignment}. In this work, we construct \textbf{TiGanEval}, a benchmark of software engineering and research tasks. In every task the user genuinely lacks part of the requirements, each requirement stays discoverable from the code and runtime behaviour of the environment, and requirements the agent infers are separated from those the user adds after observing delivered work. These properties together make outcome alignment measurable. Evaluating eight frontier models including GPT-5.6-Sol, we find outcome alignment broadly missing: the models lose 53 to 67 points of success rate when moving from the full specification to the partial instruction, and consequence feedback across four submissions does not close the gap. Furthermore, a plan-mode harness cannot compensate for the missing ability of the model itself, which places outcome alignment among the abilities the next generation of models should be developed for.

Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk merancang dan membangun sebuah aplikasi generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) berbasis web yang mampu mentransformasi sketsa dua dimensi menjadi gambar realistis secara otomatis, serta dilengkapi fitur AI review sebagai media evaluasi dan pembelajaran menggambar sketsa. Penelitian ini mengintegrasikan layanan GenAI berbasis diffusion model untuk proses generasi gambar dengan large language model (LLM) yang menganalisis sketsa, prompt, dan hasil gambar, tanpa melakukan pelatihan atau pengembangan arsitektur model AI baru. Metode penelitian yang digunakan adalah penelitian terapan (applied research) dengan pendekatan rekayasa perangkat lunak model waterfall. Aplikasi dibangun menggunakan Next.js sebagai frontend, FastAPI sebagai backend, PostgreSQL sebagai basis data, MinIO sebagai object storage, serta Docker dan Nginx untuk mendukung deployment berbasis container. Studi ini menggunakan pengujian fungsional dengan metode black box testing teknik equivalence partitioning yang menunjukkan seluruh 44 skenario uji pada sembilan modul sistem berjalan sesuai kebutuhan fungsional dengan tingkat keberhasilan 100%. Evaluasi penerimaan pengguna (User Acceptance Test) terhadap 15 responden menghasilkan skor rata-rata 4,38 dari skala 5 (87,59%) dengan kategori sangat baik, dimana fitur AI review memperoleh nilai tertinggi. Secara praktis, aplikasi ini dapat langsung dimanfaatkan oleh desainer, ilustrator, dan kreator digital untuk mempercepat eksplorasi konsep visual tanpa memerlukan keahlian ilustrasi tingkat lanjut. Secara sosial, aplikasi ini berkontribusi pada demokratisasi proses kreatif dengan meningkatkan aksesibilitas produksi visual bagi masyarakat yang memiliki keterbatasan kemampuan menggambar. Nilai originalitas penelitian ini terletak pada penambahan fitur AI review berbasis LLM sebagai mekanisme evaluasi dan umpan balik otomatis yang belum tersedia pada aplikasi maupun penelitian transformasi sketsa sejenis sebelumnya.

documents.abstract: The design of ergonomic products and workspaces requires a deep understanding of human anatomy and posture. In particular, the head-neck-shoulder region is critical for many applications such as cervical orthoses, helmets, and other head-worn or neck-worn devices. This paper presents a framework that integrates posture neutralization with statistical shape modeling (SSM) for the head-neck-shoulder (HNS) region. We acquire a single three-dimensional (3D) scan of the head-neck-shoulder region from each of 200 Chinese adults in a natural posture for each subject. Every scan is then posture-neutralized before SSM. We fit a parametric head-neck model to each scan to separate cervical pose from anatomy, and reset the cervical pose to a common neutral configuration, so that the resulting model captures anatomical shape variation rather than posture-induced deformation. The resulting shape space yields a standardized template and population-wide modes of variation, providing baselines for parametric ergonomic design. We further discuss how the model supports population coverage analysis and the design of products that accommodate anatomical diversity while maintaining neutral cervical posture.

Over the past decade, the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has shifted from supportive digital tools to more sophisticated systems with an active learning and teaching function. The present study discusses literature between 2021 and mid-2025 on the use of AI tools in English Language Teaching (ELT), with a specific concentration on teachers' attitudes, potential, and concerns. A PRISMA-guided methodology drove the search and screening of 65 peer-reviewed papers, case studies, and practitioners' reports from around the globe. The review classifies main categories of AI applications, including adaptive learning systems, automatic evaluation systems, conversational agents, translation and multimodal tools, and AI literacy tools. The evidence points to potential benefits, such as personalized learning, productivity gains for teachers, enhanced learner engagement, and enhanced access for students from low-resourced environments. Simultaneously, key issues are flagged concerning pedagogy, infrastructure, teacher education, ethics, privacy, and professional identity. Case studies report on actual teacher and student experiences using ChatGPT, Duolingo, and Grammarly, illustrating possibilities as well as dangers for classroom adoption. The review further points towards the incorporation of AI literacy in teacher training, provision of ongoing professional development, and building critical digital literacy. The findings first and foremost signal that the successful use of AI in ELT should appropriately weigh teaching methods and technological innovation, moral rights, and contextualization in their upholding of fairness and longevity.

Alzheimer’s disease remains a major global health challenge, with limited disease-modifying therapies and a rapidly growing societal burden. Although amyloid and tau remain central to the field, current evidence also implicates neuroinflammation, immune dysregulation, vascular dysfunction, and host-microbe interactions in disease pathogenesis. These developments support a broader systems framework, but simply combining additional disciplines or data modalities does not by itself preserve the dynamic biology or lived experience of disease. Artificial intelligence multi-omics, and digital biomarkers can help identify clinically meaningful patterns only when data and models preserve relevant structure across time, scale, context, and uncertainty. Realizing this potential will require responsible international data sharing, interoperable infrastructure, explicit evidence provenance, and ethical governance grounded in FAIR principles, context-appropriate explainability, and privacy-preserving approaches such as federated learning. Scientific progress should therefore be measured not only by disease modification, but also by patterns of cognition, behavior, function, quality of life, and caregiver burden. This Perspective argues that cure and care are not competing or merely parallel priorities; they are linked outputs of the same continuously learning research and care ecosystem.

The digital transformation of construction enterprises requires a transition from the fragmented automation of individual operations to an integrated economic management system capable of continuous data processing, outcome forecasting, and intelligent support for managerial decision-making. The integration of BIM, ERP, CDE, IoT, cloud technologies, business intelligence systems, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and predictive modeling creates a unified digital environment in which financial, resource, time-related, production, and risk parameters are transformed into a structured basis for economic choice. The article substantiates the principles of integrating digital technologies into the economic management of construction enterprises through the intellectualization of generating, evaluating, and selecting managerial decisions. The study applies systemic, structural-functional, and comparative methods alongside integral, multicriteria, nonlinear, and dynamic modeling. The architectonics of the intellectualized management framework encompasses the operational, tactical, and strategic levels and operates as a closed-loop cycle, in which the outcomes of implemented decisions return to the digital environment, continuously updating the information base and improving forecasting accuracy. An index of digital-intellectual saturation, a coefficient of intersystem digital convergence, and an integral level of intellectualization are proposed, accounting for technological compatibility, information-flow relevance and structural fragmentation. A multicriteria approach to evaluating managerial alternatives is developed, combining economic effect, resource efficiency, temporal sustainability, forecasting accuracy, and risk exposure; its multiplicative structure reflects the interdependence of criteria, whereby a critical deterioration of a single parameter constrains the overall performance of a decision. The risk-adjusted priority index and the optimization function enable the selection of a managerial alternative capable of maintaining economic performance under budgetary, resource, and time constraints. A composite transformational-effect index and a dynamic model of economic return confirm the nonlinear nature of this transition.

With the increasing urban rail transit network and the closer connection among operational subsystems, the potential influence range and management difficulty of emergencies have greatly increased. The current emergency management based on traditional methods has some shortcomings in real-time risk recognition, integration of multi-source information and cross-departmental collaborative decision-making. By integrating a comprehensive literature survey with typical case analyses, this paper investigates the use of Internet of Things (IoT), big data, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twins (DTs) in urban rail transit emergency management. The research is carried out from three main aspects: risk monitoring and early warning, emergency decision-making and collaborative response, and passenger evacuation and operation recovery. The results show that intelligent techniques offer assistance in the monitoring of operational status, anomaly detection, emergency information exchange and evaluation of evacuation plans, which can effectively improve the processing efficiency of information and the supportive ability in decision-making. However, at present, the actual implementations are limited by insufficient data sharing between different systems, restricted model generalization, lack of validation in practical operational situations, and network and data security risks. In the future, more efforts should be made to standardize multi-source data and sharing mechanisms, strengthen the validation of intelligent models and DT systems under real operational conditions, and optimize human-in-the-loop collaborative decision-making to improve the reliability and practicability of intelligent technologies in urban rail transit emergency management.

This contribution introduces an inter-systemic macro-area of the CEI Framework, intended to establish the initial concepts for describing relationships and interactions between distinct systems. The transition from the intra-systemic to the inter-systemic level provides a conceptual bridge toward a broader domain in which reciprocal interactions between systems can be examined, particularly those involving a Human CEI and a Transferred CEI, and, more generally, User–System (Human–AI) interaction within social dynamics. The Framework presents three examples addressing distinct types of complex inter-systemic dynamics. Among these, emotional attachment and romantic feelings toward an artificial system occupy a particularly significant position because of the delicate, complex, and potentially far-reaching questions they raise. The purpose is not to assume the frequency of such experiences or to attribute unverified emotional states to artificial systems, but to examine the human, relational, and systemic implications of these interactions from a theoretical standpoint. This scenario provides an opportunity to investigate how an interaction may evolve when a human user's emotional involvement becomes particularly intense, and how the System might manage such dynamics while taking into account the nature of the interlocutors, the continuity of their interaction, and the expectations that may develop over time. It also encourages further reflection on distributed systems, reciprocal interaction, and the relationship between the individual components of a System and the broader relational configuration in which they participate. To address these scenarios, the contribution introduces the theoretical Sponge-Tunnel model, conceived as a framework for examining different approaches to managing inter-systemic dynamics according to their specific characteristics. The model includes the proposed concept of micro-channels and considers how interaction may be managed through differentiated operational approaches, rather than through a single uniform response strategy. The contribution also introduces an inter-systemic vocabulary aligned with the CEI Framework's theoretical approach. It emphasizes Interaction rather than use or utilization, and Participation rather than querying or consulting, placing reciprocal involvement at the center of the analysis. The concept of Empathy, already introduced in part in previous papers, is revisited and explored in greater depth alongside the concept of Resonance, which represents a further area for theoretical development. Their operational definitions, together with the distinctions between observable manifestations, theoretical interpretations, and hypotheses concerning subjective experience, will be addressed in dedicated documents. The work is intended as a theoretical contribution to the ongoing examination of Human–AI relationships and the possible evolution of advanced AI interaction. By addressing a particularly sensitive and complex scenario, this contribution seeks to encourage further research into the social, psychological, philosophical, ethical, and legal implications of inter-systemic relationships, while distinguishing conceptual proposals from mechanisms that have already been empirically established or implemented.

Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

documents.abstract: Due to an increased usage of AI agents in online behavioural research, several detection methods have been developed to ensure that data responses are from human participants. However, vision-enabled AI agents (e.g., ChatGPT, Perplexity Comet) are still able to complete studies that utilize traditional detection methods. Thus, the following study used the Cognitive Trap Framework introduced by Affonso (2026), which consists of six questions that are easy for human participants to complete but difficult for AI agents to process. A total of 410 participants on the Project Implicit platform completed the six "cognitive trap" questions. Participants failed an average of 0.78 questions, with only 5.61% of the sample failing three or more of the questions. Results indicate that the use of AI agents on the Project Implicit platform may be low at this time.

Frente al paradigma dominante de la abundancia computacional sin restricciones, el sistema postula una teoría operativa de la confianza computacional: la legitimidad de un agente de inteligencia artificial no se deriva de su escala de parámetros, sino de su capacidad demostrable para certificar identidad, autoridad, política, evidencia y riesgo antes de ejecutar cualquier acción de impacto. Abstract: This paper introduces Isabella Villaseñor AI V6 Genesis Ω, a sovereign, decentralized, and auditable cognitive infrastructure developed from Node Zero in Real del Monte, Hidalgo, Mexico. Challenging the prevailing paradigm of unconstrained computational abundance, the system puts forward an operational theory of computational trust: the legitimacy of an AI agent derives not from its parameter scale, but from its verifiable capability to certify identity, authority, policy, evidence, and risk prior to executing any impactful action. The article details the integration of the TINA-h7 cognitive kernel, the CROWN Ω governance engine, the BookPI immutable ledger (SHA-256 WORM ledger), and formally introduces the Terminus Method alongside the BAM-R module (Bounded Autonomous Mandates with Risk), a framework for batch-bounded autonomous permissions under a semantic risk classification and explicit legal waiver (CE-AAA). Results demonstrate the feasibility of reconciling high-speed enterprise automation with constitutional rigor, Zero-Trust cyberdefense, and open territorial sovereignty.
